my_independent_answer: You don't lose the instant you attempt the draw; it's a state-based action, so you lose the next time SBAs are checked, which happens before any player would receive priority (704.5b, 121.4).
answer_note: Both cited rules verified verbatim and support the timing claim precisely.
question_note: Clear question with one correct answer; discriminates between systems that know the SBA-timing nuance vs. those that just say 'you lose.'

my_independent_answer: Combat has 5 steps in fixed order (506.1). Priority in each step: the active player receives priority first (117.3a). The defending player (in a 2-player game, the only other player) gets priority only after the active player acts and that action resolves (117.3b), or after the active player passes with nothing on the stack (117.3d: 'the next player in turn order receives priority'). A correct answer needs 117.3d (and ideally 117.3b) to actually explain defending-player priority, not 117.3a alone.

my_independent_answer: Layers are the fixed order (613.1) in which continuous effects are applied to determine an object's characteristics: 1 copiable values, 2 control, 3 text, 4 type, 5 color, 6 abilities/keyword counters, 7 power/toughness, generally in timestamp order within a layer (with layers 1 and 7 split into sublayers, and dependency able to override timestamp order).

my_independent_answer: If one player controls two+ legendary permanents with the exact same name, that player picks one to keep and the rest go to their owners' graveyards (704.5j, the 'legend rule'). It's per-controller and per-name, so different players or different names don't trigger it.
answer_note: 704.5j verified verbatim; the added clarifications (different players okay, different names okay) are correct restatements of the rule's conditions, not extra claims needing separate citation.
question_note: Common, well-defined rules question with one correct answer.
cr_evidence: 704.5j If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. This is called the “legend rule.”

my_independent_answer: Not instantly -- lethal damage causes destruction as a state-based action (704.5g, 302.7), so it's checked (and the creature actually dies) the next time SBAs are checked, i.e. right before any player would get priority. There can be a window where lethal damage is marked but the creature hasn't died yet.
answer_note: Both rules verified verbatim; directly support the timing claim.

my_independent_answer: No direct cast from exile -- 903.8 only allows casting a commander from the command zone. If a commander is put into exile (or graveyard) since the last SBA check, its owner may move it to the command zone as a state-based action (903.9a), optional, and from there it can be cast (paying the commander tax again). So it always routes through the command zone, never a direct exile-cast.
answer_note: Both rules verified verbatim; the answer correctly identifies there's no direct exile-cast permission and explains the actual path back via 903.9a.
question_note: Presumes Commander format, but the question is naturally read as Commander-specific (commander is a Commander-only concept), so this isn't a false premise -- it's an implicit-format question, standard for commander-rules queries. Fine as an eval question.
cr_evidence: 903.8. A player may cast a commander they own from the command zone. / 903.9a If a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. This is a state-based action.

my_independent_answer: Two turn-based actions happen automatically: (1) active player discards down to max hand size if over it (514.1), (2) simultaneously, all damage is removed and 'until end of turn'/'this turn' effects end (514.2). Normally no player gets priority in cleanup, so no spells/abilities (514.3) -- BUT if an SBA would need to be performed or a triggered ability is waiting to go on the stack (including 'at the beginning of the next cleanup step' triggers), those are handled, the active player gets priority, a normal priority round happens, and then another cleanup step begins once the stack empties and everyone passes (514.3a). So the answer must include 514.3/514.3a to be complete -- omitting them leaves out exactly the mechanism that lets anything happen beyond the two automatic actions.
